Hitler's War

Britain Alone, and Hitler Turns East

Mr. MagisterYour teacher
Today's Focus

By the end of June 1940 Hitler ruled from the Atlantic to the Soviet border, and only Britain still fought him. Many people expected Britain to make peace. It did not. This lesson asks why Britain held out, how it survived the summer, and why Hitler then turned east against the Soviet Union, the same country that had helped him divide Poland. Finish your two-column list on Dunkirk as you read.

Objectives
  1. Explain why Britain chose to fight on in 1940 and how the Battle of Britain was won.
  2. Describe how the United States helped Britain while it stayed officially neutral.
  3. Explain why Hitler attacked the Soviet Union in 1941 and what happened in the first months.
Quick Check-in

One country will not make peace and keeps fighting. What do you think its enemy will try next?

Historical Figure
Winston ChurchillWIN-stun CHUR-chil

Winston Churchill (1874 to 1965) was born at Blenheim Palace into one of England’s great families. He was a soldier and a newspaper reporter before he entered Parliament in 1900. He served as head of the navy before the Great War, and he took the blame for the failed Gallipoli campaign in 1915.

In the 1930s he was out of office, and he warned that Hitler was a danger while most of his party hoped for peace. He became prime minister on May 10, 1940, at the age of sixty-five. His speeches gave the country courage, and his stubbornness kept it in the fight. Voters turned him out in the election of 1945, but he returned as prime minister from 1951 to 1955. He wrote many books, and in 1953 he won the Nobel Prize in Literature.

In the War Cabinet

Battle
The Battle of Britain

The battle took place in the skies over southern England and the Channel. The Luftwaffe had about 2,500 aircraft ready for the attack, and the RAF had a few hundred fighters. The two fighters that met most often were the British Spitfire and Hurricane and the German Messerschmitt 109.

Pilots on both sides flew several times a day, and many were killed. The Germans lost far more aircraft than the British, and they could not replace their trained crews fast enough. The battle ended in October when the Luftwaffe turned to night raids and the invasion was shelved. It was the first major German defeat of the war.

Part 1

Britain Holds Out

Chapter 1The Choice in London
Chapter 2The Battle of Britain
Chapter 1

The Choice in London

While the army was still trapped at Dunkirk, the small War Cabinet argued about whether to ask for terms. Lord Halifax wanted to see what Hitler would offer, perhaps through Mussolini. Winston Churchill said no. He believed that any terms would leave Britain helpless, and Hitler’s breach of the Munich promise had shown what his word was worth. Churchill also spoke to the larger group of ministers outside the cabinet, and they cheered him. The argument ended in his favor on May 28.

Think about how close it was. France sought an armistice a few weeks later, and many of Britain’s leaders were tired, short of arms, and afraid of bombing. Britain’s army had come home with its rifles but not its guns, and the expeditionary force that had crossed to France in the autumn was in pieces. A cabinet led by a man who preferred a settlement would probably have taken one. Churchill did not seem to stand for any such comfort. He had a gift for words, but what mattered more was his steady nerve.

Chapter 2

The Battle of Britain

Hitler hoped that Britain would give in. When it did not, he ordered his generals to prepare an invasion across the Channel, named Sea Lion. A crossing would be dangerous without air superiority. German barges could not live under the guns of the Royal Navy, and bombers could hold off the navy only if the RAF was beaten first. So the Luftwaffe began the Battle of Britain in July 1940, first attacking shipping in the Channel and then the airfields of RAF Fighter Command.

Fighter Command had fewer pilots, but it had advantages. Its chief, Air Chief Marshal Hugh Dowding, had built a system that joined the radar stations you met in the previous module to the telephone lines and the control rooms. Fighters took off only when and where they were needed. British pilots fought over their own soil, so a pilot who parachuted could fly again the next day. Pilots from Poland and Czechoslovakia, who had escaped after their countries fell, flew among them.

By early September the airfields were near their limit. Then Hitler made a mistake. After a few German bombs fell on London by accident and the RAF answered with a raid on Berlin, he turned his bombers on London itself. On September 7 the Blitz began. The airfields had time to recover. On September 15 the Luftwaffe sent its biggest raid yet and lost many planes. Two days later Hitler put Sea Lion off, and it was never revived. Churchill said of the pilots that “never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few.”

Part 2

The Blitz and the Wider War

Chapter 3The Blitz and the Help from America
Chapter 4The Wider War
Chapter 3

The Blitz and the Help from America

The Blitz went on until May 1941. London was bombed on fifty-seven nights in a row, and Coventry and other cities were struck as well. More than 40,000 British civilians died. Hitler hoped that fear would turn the people against their government. It did not, because most Britons grew angrier, not weaker.

Britain needed help, and only the United States could give it. American law still required neutrality, and many Americans wanted to stay out of the war. President Franklin Roosevelt found ways to help anyway. In September 1940 he traded fifty old destroyers to Britain for bases in the Caribbean. After he won a third term that November, he called America the “arsenal of democracy.” In March 1941 Congress passed Lend-Lease, which let him send war supplies without payment on the spot. Britain was nearly out of money, and without this aid it could not have kept buying what it needed.

Chapter 4

The Wider War

In September 1940 Germany, Italy, and Japan signed a pact of mutual support. The three powers were called the Axis. Mussolini, eager for glory, invaded Greece in October, and the Greeks drove his army back. Hitler then had to rescue his partner. In April 1941 German troops overran Yugoslavia and Greece, and a small British force that had landed to help the Greeks had to be taken off again. In May German paratroopers took Crete. In North Africa the British had beaten the Italians, but a German general named Erwin Rommel arrived in February 1941 and drove them back.

Part 3

Hitler Turns East

Chapter 5Why Hitler Turned East
Chapter 6The First Six Months
Chapter 5

Why Hitler Turned East

Why did Hitler attack Russia while Britain still fought? He had told his generals in July 1940 that Britain was holding out in hope of Soviet help, so that smashing Russia would take away Britain’s last hope and keep America out. He also believed what he had written years before: Germany needed land in the east, and Communism was his deadly enemy. And he thought the Red Army weak, after Stalin’s purge of its officers and the poor Soviet showing in Finland. “You have only to kick in the door,” he is reported to have said, “and the whole rotten structure will come crashing down.”

On December 18, 1940 he signed Directive No. 21, which you will read in this module. The plan was a larger Sichelschnitt. Armored wedges would drive deep into Russia and surround the Soviet armies before they could retreat. It was named Barbarossa, for a medieval German emperor. The date was set for May 1941, and the invasion was postponed to June 22 in part because the Balkan campaign came first. About three million German soldiers, with allies from Romania, Finland, and Hungary, stood along the border.

Stalin had been warned. British intelligence, spies in Tokyo and Berlin, and even a German deserter told him an attack was coming. He did not believe it, or did not want to. He feared that moving his army would give Hitler a reason to strike, and Soviet trains kept carrying grain and oil to Germany until the last night.

Chapter 6

The First Six Months

On June 22, 1941, the Luftwaffe destroyed over a thousand Soviet aircraft in a day, many of them on the ground. Panzer groups encircled Soviet armies at Minsk and Smolensk. At Kiev in September, over half a million Soviet soldiers were taken. By October the Germans were within sight of Moscow. Then the autumn rains turned the roads to mud, supplies ran short, and the cold came before the winter clothing did. Fresh Soviet divisions, some brought from Siberia, struck back on December 5 and pushed the Germans away from the city.

Notice how this changed the war. Hitler had planned a lightning campaign, and he now faced a long war on two fronts against two vast countries. That was the thing German leaders had feared since 1914. Consider whether he could have beaten Britain first, or waited until Britain was weaker. Write your own judgment in your notebook, and use it in this module’s discussion.
